stem: A 23-year-old woman has worn latex gloves daily for 2 years as a nursing assistant. Two days after a long shift, she has itchy, red, swollen skin on both hands and wrists that stops sharply at the glove line. She has no wheeze, fever or joint pain.
oneliner: 23F + latex gloves for 2 years + itchy red swollen hands to the glove line 2 days after a shift → ?
ask: Which hypersensitivity mechanism is most likely?

options.B: Type II (antibody to cell or matrix antigen)

whyNot.A: Type I appears **within minutes** of contact; her rash appeared 2 days after the shift
whyNot.B: Type II needs **antibody against a cell or matrix antigen** (hemolysis, cytopenia, one target organ); she has a rash only where the gloves touched
whyNot.C: Type III is **systemic, with fever, joint pain and low complement**; she has none of these
whyNot.E: Direct mast cell activation is **immediate and needs no sensitization**; her rash appeared 2 days after exposure

why: A rash confined to the area of contact that appears 48 to 72 hours later means **sensitized T cells** have been recalled to the skin. Latex can cause both type IV and type I reactions; the timing tells them apart.

Timing
Typical lesion or test
Classic examples
rows: IgE on mast cells; histamine and tryptase release
Wheals and wheeze; skin prick test, raised tryptase
Anaphylaxis, hay fever, asthma, food allergy
Type II (antibody to cell or matrix antigen)
**IgG or IgM against a cell-surface or matrix antigen**, complement
Rh and ABO hemolysis, Goodpasture, Graves, myasthenia gravis
1 to 2 weeks after first exposure; hours on re-exposure (Arthus)
**Granular, lumpy deposits; low C3 and C4**
Serum sickness, SLE, post-streptococcal GN, polyarteritis nodosa
Vesicles or induration; patch test, tuberculin
Poison ivy, nickel, tuberculin test, GVHD

idea.rule: Rash at the contact site 2 to 3 days later = type IV, T cell mediated.
also: Nickel, latex, poison ivy and the tuberculin test are all type IV

set_title: Pain, blood or a lump at the anus: tear, swollen vein, wart or cancer
stem: A 31-year-old man has had 3 months of anal itching and a growth at the anal verge. He has HIV infection. Condyloma acuminatum and anal squamous cell carcinoma are both being considered.
oneliner: 31M + HIV infection + 3 months of itching + growth at the anal verge → Condyloma acuminatum or anal squamous cell carcinoma?
ask: Which single finding favours condyloma acuminatum over anal squamous cell carcinoma?

options.A: A firm ulcerated surface with induration
options.B: Enlarged, firm superficial inguinal lymph nodes
options.E: Greater frequency in patients with HIV infection

whyNot.A: A firm ulcerated surface with induration points to **carcinoma**
whyNot.B: Enlarged firm inguinal nodes point to **carcinoma** spreading to the superficial inguinal nodes
whyNot.C: Both are **HPV-related** (types 6 and 11 versus 16 and 18), so this does not separate them
whyNot.E: HIV is **already in the stem** and raises the frequency of both

why: Both lesions are HPV-related and more frequent with HIV. **Multiple soft, cauliflower-like warts** (low-risk HPV 6 and 11) are benign condylomata, whereas carcinoma from HPV 16 and 18 forms a firm, ulcerated mass.

Bleeding
What is seen
Relation to the dentate line

**Single tense, tender, bluish lump at the anal verge**

Mild or absent early; worse with sphincter invasion
At or below the line; drains to the superficial inguinal nodes; HPV 16 and 18
Perianal skin and anal canal; HPV 6 and 11

idea.rule: Several soft cauliflower-like warts = condyloma (HPV 6, 11); a single hard ulcerated mass = carcinoma (HPV 16, 18).
also: Acetowhitening with acetic acid highlights the lesions

The quadrivalent and nonavalent vaccines prevent both

set_title: Pale skin, hair or eyes from birth, or white patches: no melanin, no melanocytes or destroyed melanocytes
stem: A 31-year-old woman with hypothyroidism has noticed milk-white patches on her hands and around her mouth that have enlarged during the past year. A biopsy of a patch shows no melanocytes.
oneliner: 31F + hypothyroidism + enlarging milk-white patches around the mouth and on the hands over a year + biopsy with no melanocytes → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Chediak-Higashi syndrome shows light skin and silvery hair from infancy with recurrent infections; her patches **began in adulthood and enlarged over a year**
whyNot.B: Oculocutaneous albinism gives diffuse pallor from birth with nystagmus; hers are **patches that enlarged over a year in adulthood**
whyNot.D: Waardenburg syndrome is present from birth with deafness; her patches **began in adulthood**
whyNot.E: Piebaldism gives fixed patches from birth; hers **enlarged over the past year**

why: Autoreactive T cells destroy melanocytes, leaving sharply bordered, milk-white patches that spread over time. It clusters with autoimmune thyroid disease and type 1 diabetes. **Acquired, enlarging white patches with no melanocytes in an adult with autoimmune thyroid disease** is vitiligo.

head: Pattern of pale skin
Melanocytes
Eyes and ears
Other clue and inheritance
rows: **Diffuse pale skin and hair from birth**
Normal in number but little or no melanin (tyrosinase defect)
Autosomal recessive; sunburn and skin cancer risk
Missing in the patches (neural crest defect)
**Sensorineural deafness, heterochromia and wide-set inner canthi**
**Fixed white forelock and patches on the forehead, chest and abdomen from birth**
Starts after infancy; linked to autoimmune thyroid disease and type 1 diabetes
Present, but melanosome trafficking is abnormal (LYST defect)
**Recurrent pyogenic infections, giant granules in neutrophils and neuropathy**; autosomal recessive

idea.rule: Acquired, enlarging, sharply bordered white patches with absent melanocytes and autoimmune disease = vitiligo.
also: Melanocytes were present and then destroyed, unlike piebaldism where they never arrived
Wood lamp makes the patches brighter

set_title: Patchy hair loss in a young person: pulling, autoimmune, shedding, hormones or fungus
stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought by his mother because of 4 months of hair loss. He has been withdrawn since his parents separated. Examination shows two round, completely smooth, hairless patches with short tapered hairs at the edges, over normal-appearing skin.
oneliner: 12M + 4 months of hair loss + round smooth hairless patches with short tapered hairs at the edges → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Tinea capitis gives a scaly, inflamed patch; his **scalp skin is normal**
whyNot.B: Trichotillomania gives irregular patches with hairs of different lengths; his patches are **round and completely smooth**
whyNot.D: Telogen effluvium is diffuse shedding; he has **two round, hairless patches**
whyNot.E: Androgenetic alopecia gives hairline recession and crown thinning; he has **two round, smooth patches**

why: Alopecia areata is a T cell-mediated autoimmune attack on hair follicles that spares the stem cells, so hair can regrow. The changed sentence is the clue: **round, smooth, hairless patches with short tapered hairs at the edges over normal skin**.

set_title: Patchy hair loss in a young person: pulling, autoimmune, shedding, hormones or fungus
stem: A 31-year-old woman has had 6 weeks of heavy hair shedding, with hair in the shower drain and on her pillow. She delivered her first child 3 months ago. Examination shows diffuse thinning over the whole scalp with no bare patches and normal skin.
oneliner: 31F + heavy hair shedding 3 months after delivery + diffuse thinning with no bare patches → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Trichotillomania gives irregular patches; she has **diffuse shedding over the whole scalp with no patches**
whyNot.B: Tinea capitis gives a scaly patch; her **scalp skin is normal and the loss is diffuse**
whyNot.C: Androgenetic alopecia thins gradually at the temples and crown; hers is **6 weeks of heavy shedding 3 months after delivery**
whyNot.E: Alopecia areata gives discrete bare patches; she has **no bare patches**

why: Childbirth, high fever or surgery pushes many follicles into the resting (telogen) phase together, and they shed about 2 to 3 months later. **Diffuse shedding 3 months after delivery with no bare patches** is telogen effluvium, and the hair regrows.

set_title: Patchy hair loss in a young person: pulling, autoimmune, shedding, hormones or fungus
stem: A 29-year-old man has noticed his hairline slowly receding over 5 years. Examination shows recession at both temples and thinning over the crown, with normal-appearing scalp skin. His father was bald by age 35.
oneliner: 29M + hairline receding over 5 years + temple recession and crown thinning + bald father → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Telogen effluvium is diffuse shedding a few months after a stressor; he has **slow temple recession and crown thinning over 5 years**
whyNot.B: Alopecia areata gives round, smooth bare patches over weeks; his hairline recedes **slowly over 5 years at the temples and crown**
whyNot.C: Trichotillomania gives irregular patches with hairs of different lengths; he has **symmetric recession at the temples and crown**
whyNot.D: Tinea capitis gives a scaly patch; his **scalp skin is normal**

why: Dihydrotestosterone shrinks hair follicles (miniaturization) in a pattern of temple recession and crown thinning, and family history is common. **Slow temple recession and crown thinning with a bald father** is androgenetic alopecia; finasteride or topical minoxidil can be used.

set_title: Patchy hair loss in a young person: pulling, autoimmune, shedding, hormones or fungus
stem: A 5-year-old girl has had 3 weeks of an itchy patch of hair loss. Examination shows a scaly, red 3-cm patch with hairs broken off at the scalp surface and tender enlarged lymph nodes at the back of the neck.
oneliner: 5F + 3 weeks of itchy hair loss + scaly red patch with broken hairs + tender posterior neck nodes → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Trichotillomania gives irregular patches over normal skin; her scalp is **scaly and red with tender nodes**
whyNot.C: Telogen effluvium is diffuse shedding; she has **a single scaly patch**
whyNot.D: Alopecia areata gives smooth bare patches without scale; her patch is **scaly and red with broken hairs**
whyNot.E: Androgenetic alopecia thins gradually at the temples and crown; she has **a single scaly red patch with tender nodes**

why: Dermatophytes such as Trichophyton tonsurans invade the hair shaft. **A scaly, itchy patch with hairs broken at the scalp and tender posterior cervical nodes** is tinea capitis; KOH shows hyphae, and oral griseofulvin or terbinafine is needed because topical agents do not reach the follicle.
